utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin today, I'd like to deal with several administrative matters first. First, the Chamber will issue a short oral ruling in relation to the Prosecution motion for stay of the Chamber's decision on the accused's motion to unseal the ICMP exhibits and for extension of time filed on the 2nd of May, 2012. Having considered the arguments in the motion, as well as the accused's response to it, the Chamber has decided to temporarily stay its decision on the accused's motion to unseal ICMP exhibits which was issued on the 25th of April, 2012, and to grant the extension of time sought by the Prosecution in order to allow it to redact some of the ICMP exhibits in accordance with that decision. The Chamber's decision will therefore be stayed until the 18th of May, 2012, by which time the Prosecution shall both report back to the Chamber on its dealings with the ICMP, regarding the ICMP exhibits, and will also complete the exercise of redacting some of the said exhibits. Next, on the 2nd of May, 2012, the accused filed a request to append translation report to Exhibit P967, i.e., directive 4. I'm wondering whether Prosecution wishes to respond to the accused's request. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That wasn't on our list of anticipated responses, Mr. President. But if you give me a moment to revisit that filing, I will give you a definitive response by the -- in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will come to the last issue. In any event, could you come back to us after the first break. Yes. As the Prosecution's case is drawing to a close, the Chamber would benefit from hearing from the parties as to whether they are of the position that the Chamber's decision on designation on stand-by counsel issued on the 15th of April, 2010, should continue to apply after the close of the Prosecution's case, and, if so, to what extent. The Chamber, therefore, requests that the parties, as well as Mr. Harvey, file their written submission on this topic no later than Friday, 11th of May, 2012. My apologies, Mr. Witness, for your inconvenience. If the witness would take the solemn declaration, please. Sir, do you follow the proceedings in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. As an initial matter, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the witness is unfortunately suffering from a very bad toothache. We were notified of that this morning. He has decided that he wants to go through with this, get this over, and then that will be dealt with. But in the event that we have to take additional breaks, that is the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. And thank you for your co-operation, sir. If you feel uncomfortable any time, please don't hesitate to let us know. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 90332, not to be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at the screen in front of you and without reading anything or -- out loud, can you please confirm from [sic] us whether that is your name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5027, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you testified in the Popovic case in 2000 -- in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you have listened to your testimony, that it's accurate, and if asked the same questions today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I have nothing else to say but what I saw with my own eyes and what I went through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 22712A as the public version, and 22712 under seal. We are only tendering three associated exhibits. They are just three photographs; that's 14086, 14087, 14109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the excerpt from video.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're not tendering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objections, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we ... yes, we receive both versions Popovic transcript as well as three associated exhibits. Shall we give the numbers now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 22712A will be Exhibit P5028, under seal. And 65 ter 22712B will be Exhibit P5029. 65 ter 14086 will be Exhibit P5030. 65 ter 14087 will be Exhibit P5031. And 65 ter 14109 will be Exhibit P5032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a brief summary. The witness survived a mass execution of Muslim men and boys at the Kravica warehouse on 13 July 1995. Two days earlier, the witness had been forced to abandon his home, and his wife and daughters went to Potocari as he fled through the woods. He was forced to surrender on July 13th in the hills above the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road and was taken prisoner at a meadow. The witness heard that approximately 2.000 people had been captured there. While at the meadow, General Mladic arrived and addressed the prisoners, promising them that they would not be harmed. Shortly thereafter, the prisoners were told to line up a column, four abreast, and march towards Kravica. The witness arrived at the Kravica warehouse between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon and entered the western part of the warehouse. That side of the warehouse was nearly full and the witness sat down with his back against the wall. When the last prisoner entered, the room was so crowded that the last prisoner had no place to sit. A soldier kicked that prisoner in the lower back and demanded that he sit down. When the prisoner responded that he was unable to comply, the soldier fired at him. The witness testified that this is when the shooting started and it did not stop until it became dark. The witness took cover among the dead and lay still in the warehouse overnight in their blood. The witness remained that way for the whole following day during which time soldiers called out for the wounded prisoners, promising to take them to the hospital. Some prisoners believed the promise, went outside and were killed. Around noon, the witness could hear machinery noise outside the building and when it became night, he heard the command: "Park the loader, wash the asphalt, cover the dead with hay." Sometime after midnight, the witness escaped from the warehouse. He was joined by another survivor and fled behind the warehouse into a field of corn.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few questions for you. While you were at the meadow on that afternoon, at some point did a military truck show up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: A military truck showed up while we were seated in the meadow. They asked for 35 people to work and they -- they were loaded on the truck. The only one I knew was Fadil Husejnovic. I didn't know the rest of them. The lorry's engine turned on and they were taken into a direction unknown to me. I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Towards the end of your time at the meadow, did General Mladic appear?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: While we were in that meadow - I don't know when that was because I didn't have a watch - General Mladic came and addressed us. He asked us, Do you know me? Some said that they knew him. I kept quiet. The first word he uttered was, Naser abandoned you, and he fled to Tuzla. You are better off not waging war against Serbs. We evacuated your families to Tuzla, Kladanj and Zivinice, and most probably within a day or two, you will be exchanged and you will all find your families. Nobody will beat you. Nobody will provoke you. We will give you food. You are very hot here. We will accommodate you somewhere where it is colder. We applauded him. I raised my hand. I was barefoot. I told him, General, sir, I have my shoes in the back-pack. Can I go and fetch them? And he said, We will give you a pair of shoes. And then I said, Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you just told us what you said and it appears to be a verbatim quote. Can you tell us why you remember this so well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: It is branded in my memory. I will always remember that. I remember very well what he said when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, as you noted, your testimony in the previous case was admitted in its entirety, in lieu of your oral testimony in-chief in this case. Now you will be further asked by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and I have to remind myself that we should make pauses between questions and answers because we want everything recorded. We want to give the interpreters ample time to interpret our words. I'm not going to mention the name of your village but let me ask you: Are you natives of that village, are you indigenous there in that village or did you move from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That's where I was born. That's where I will die. I was expelled, but I have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your financial standing? What was your profession?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I was a farmer. I was engaged in cattle breeding. That was my main occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please make a pause after my question. How much land did your family have? Would you -- would you have considered -- would you consider yourself a rich family?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I had a lot of land, but there was nobody to work on that land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many head of cattle did you have during the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I had four to five cows, about 20 to 30 sheep, and a horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your village, was it part of the Bandera triangle? Is your village in that area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You served in the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, were you transferred to the reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, everyone who serves in an army becomes a reservist.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I served in Tito's army, and then, from the 18th of ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of your answer, sir. What did you say after: "... from the 18th of ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 17th of April, not 18th. The 17th of April. I was in the army. And in 1996, I served in Tito's army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, but please wait with your answer. Don't start it immediately. Is it correct that between 1966 and 1992, you were a reservist of the JNA and you were called to participate in exercises?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 17th of April, 1992, you joined the unit commanded by the man that you mentioned and you stayed there without interruption until 1996?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I did it mostly during the night because I had to attend to my cattle during day-time. And when I moved to Tuzla, I was in the logistics, providing water, food, firewood, et cetera, because I was mobilised in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean demobilised in January 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this unit later on became part of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements, you said to the commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina for collecting facts on the war, you said that the fighting had started after the Serbs attacked the village of Podgaj from the Serbian village of Derventa. Were there any fighting before the 16th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know the date when Podgaj was attacked and burned. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But was there any fighting before the 16th of May and was your units involved in the fighting and sabotage actions from the very beginning until the very end?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I think that they didn't before the 17th. Nowhere. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court D1987. It used to be MFI'd but since we now have a translation, we have it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll not broadcast this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If all the parties can see the English version, maybe we can collapse it and leave only the Serbian version, enlarge it so that the witness can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this contribution to the history of the 28th Division, or, rather, the 8th Operations Group, it was something that was drawn up by the 8 OG and look what was being done. It says from the 1st of May, a sabotage action was carried out in Zutica sector. Then some attacks were avoided. And then on the 15th of May, they participated in -- liberated the area between Osredak, Orahovica, Viogor, Bojna, Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't remember those dates. I only remember that Podgaj was attacked and people were expelled, as was Zutica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at least you please wait until the English translation of witness's answer is completed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, I'm only going to ask you if you aware of this action, regardless of the date, and you can tell me whether you do know or don't know.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I know that there was such an action but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that there was another attack on Zutica, or, rather, a sabotage action, as written here, on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about these sabotage actions off the top of my head and when they took place. I had other interests and concerns of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you were a member of that unit which virtually on a daily basis was actively involved in operations, either in attacks or in defensive actions. So you carried out a large number of operations in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on. Can we scroll up the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember combat activities of your unit in the Serbian village of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I know where that happened. A neighbour of mine was killed in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On this page, we can see that this happened on the 22nd of August, 1992. Now I think we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Don't ask me about the dates. I don't know any dates of any of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also know about a sabotage action on Besica Brdo, when you captured a 55 tank, a PAT, and other war looty [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then there was a sabotage action in Nikolici. Then an attack in the Fakovici sector where you also seized a lot of combat materiel?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how come that you are listing all these villages without mentioning the six municipalities that you have expelled people from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Mr. Witness, please, I would like to assure you that I respect all the victims and I feel remorse for them, but we need to go into all the combat activities that took place and how many people were killed during those actions prior to July 1995.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I did not take part in any of the actions. I know that both sides carried out their own actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what happened at Fakovici? There was a big operation there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, there was an action. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an attempt to return Pajici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I have not heard about that before. What is the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is Pajici or Pejici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Pajic? I know that there were two houses of the Pajic family in Bukovica. I'm not familiar with the village called Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the 7th of January, 1993. There was an operation in the Kravica sector?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbian villagers were killed in Kravica on that day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not there. I don't know how many of ours of yours got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you recognised some people later on in July 1995, some people who arrived from Visnjica. Do you remember that your unit carried out several actions against Visnjica and the last of those actions was sometime on the 22nd of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I remember when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the Lipovac and Kutezero companies from January 1993 to January 1994 were on the strength of the independent battalion Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know on whose strength those companies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to read the names and you can tell me whether you know them or not. Up to the 31st of January, 1994 - we can scroll up a little - did the following people get killed. Maho Avdic, Sead Hodzic, Salko Becirevic, Juso Medic, Adil Hasanovic, Merludin Ahmetovic [phoen]. Let me not read all of the names. Can you please look at the names. We are looking at chapter 4. Can we have that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that those people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Chapter 5. Please scroll up a little bit more. Can you see the names? Can you read the names? The names of the combatants who got killed before the 31st of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. I will leave that subject. But, in any case, that unit was very active, very courageous, the command was very good, the commanders were different. There was Zulfo among them as well as Mujo Bektic. There were different commanders; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll find that in chapter 4 of this report that ends with the year 1994. Let us leave this topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can this be admitted because we have a translation of the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with it now or leave it to be dealt with together with all the other MFI documents. Mr. Robinson. If Prosecution is in the position to respond to the accused's request to fully admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd appreciate leaving it to till later, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we leave it at that, to make a more informed decision, when -- to -- to look into the situation when it was admitted. It's better to leave it now. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between you and the Serbian villages around you -- or, rather, the Serbian villages closest to you were they under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or did they have their own control, or, rather, was there a line between you and your villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: As far as I know, those Serbian villages that I know were never under the control of Zulfo Tursunovic. As for the line, there was a line between us and them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are saying that there was a line between the villages. That you were on the one side and the others -- they were on the other. How far were they from the line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: It depended on the configuration of the terrain. At places they were 2 kilometres away. They were closest to the line near Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know each other before the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your neighbours. Your Serbian neighbours from the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I knew a lot of them. I knew a lot of people from Koprivno, Nikolici, Vasiljevici, Derventa. We knew each other and we were good neighbours. If anybody had told me that things like that would happen, I would not have believed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the war, were there any contacts, since you knew each other, were there any contacts between you? Did you trade or anything?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't remember that there were any contacts, unless somebody did it furtively. As far as I remember, nobody contacted anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're saying that when a decision was made to try and break through, through the woods, you said that the first group carried out a clearing of mines. Whose mines were those?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Those were Serbian mines. I don't know who laid them. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Serbs laid minefields between your villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes. In the woods. Not between the villages. When we started walking through the woods, there were minefields there. When we set out from Jaglici, it was only then that I saw and heard about the mines. Somebody said, Watch out, there are mines in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the actions of the 28th Division against the Serbian villages from the moment when Srebrenica had been proclaimed a protected area until July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: After it had become a protected area, I don't remember any action being taken. Anyway, it's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But why, then, did the Serbs plant mines and minefields around their villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you to say. I don't know why they did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, did you have any combat contact with the VRS in the area of Tursunovic's brigade or did you hear about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: The whole day of the 11th of July, I was gathering hay. My daughter came and asked me, What are you doing? People are leaving. Srebrenica had fallen. After I finished my work, I went home. I took some food with me and I went out to let the cattle loose. I came across my brother-in-law. I took my rucksack and I set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, how did you decide to send your family to Potocari and that you should go through the woods? Was that your choice or was that decided by someone else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: A courier came who said that women, the old people, and the children should go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari because that was the protected area. Those who were able-bodied should head for the woods and it's up to them to see if they could make it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was a courier from the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, of course, from the brigade. It wasn't my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't recorded that the able-bodied should try to make a breakthrough through the woods and they should see whether they would succeed or not.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, there was no other option. I think that only nine or ten people from my village went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I understand that it's difficult to wait, but because both of you are speaking the same language, which is to be translated by the interpreters, could you kindly put a pause before you start answering the question, Mr. Witness. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point, were you yourself in two minds whether to head for Potocari, or is it a fact that your back-pack remained on your friend's horse and that you eventually decided to opt for a breakthrough after all? Can you please wait for the interpretation to be finished. You can go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: When I parted from my family above Ravne Njive, I decided to head for Potocari, because I was too old to go to the woods. But a friend of mine came. We set off from Brestove Ravne [phoen]. My back-pack was very heavy, and he decided to take it off me and put it on his horse, and that's why I decided to follow my back-pack because I had food there and I had some clothes there, and, therefore, I decided to head for Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would anyone from the brigade hold it against you if you decided to go to Potocari rather than to stay with them? Please wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the courier leave it up to people to make their own decisions whether to head for Potocari or to the forest, or was that an information in the form of an order to gather all members of the brigade in one place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what the courier decided. Everyone made their own decisions. If I didn't have this back-pack, and if I didn't head for -- and if I did go to Potocari, I wouldn't be here today. Therefore, I decided to head for the forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to Jaglici, did you all get together with their respective brigades and were there any civilians with their brigades once you gathered in Jaglici first?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: When I arrived Jaglici, it was already night. There was a huge crowd of people there, and I joined those with whom I was more friendly, and I left Jaglici with them at 20 to 1.00. I asked Nusret Turkovic from Vrsine what time it was and he told me it was 20 to 1.00, so that's how I know when I set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you had a hunting rifle with you, that you gave to someone later on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes. I had my own hunting rifle. When I met my brother-in-law in Jaglici, he found a -- the brother of a friend of mine. He took my back-pack and I told him that I had been carrying it all the time. He took the rifle from me, but he left me my back-pack with the food and the clothes that we both had packed in it. And I never saw him again, nor the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you arrived during the night, did you then line up on the morning of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, we did line up I don't know how many times that morning in Jaglici. There was no one from the command there, though. Neither anyone from the municipality. People were just wandering around randomly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did all members of all the brigades, pursuant to instruction, head off to make a breakthrough through the forest or did any of the brigades remain behind?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: The majority of civilians who were not armed were the last to leave Jaglici, and I was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at the head of the column there was a reconnaissance party, those who were clearing mines, and Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on at the head of the column. I was at the rear. Had I been closer to the head, we -- I wouldn't have found myself in dire straits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was in the command of the rear of the column? And please wait for the interpretation to finish. Go on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, nobody was in command. When we arrived at Buljim, on a macadam road, there was a valley full of people and I don't know what they were waiting for. They could not join up with the column. That was the first time that I saw Golic. Golic arrived and shouted at us, What are you waiting for? And maybe 100 metres away somebody said, We cannot find where the column went. And then he cursed his mother and his father and said, You will see where the column is, and then he headed towards that person who said that he lost the column. And he shouted from the left part of the hilltop, he started cursing and asking what the people were waiting for. And then the shooting started and nobody watched anybody else. Nobody watched me or anybody else. There was shooting, big time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time that the shooting started for the first time? Who was it that opened fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That was our first ambush that we encountered near Buljim. That was the first ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that before that, you had realised that the Serbs could see you but that they didn't open fire until you reached Buljim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know whether they saw us or not. I couldn't see what was happening in the forest and who was hiding there. When we entered the area near Buljim along the brook, the shooting started. The fire opened and then we started walking. Me and a few of my acquaintances, we started walking along the brook and I saw a lot of people who were either wounded or dead on the -- on the ground. We started walking along the brook. A neighbour caught up with me. He has a wife in Kamenica. He asked me where we were. And he told us we were near Kamenica and he told us to go left. And from that river, we turned into the wood on the left, and the dark caught up with us and then shooting started again under a hilltop. When Praga opened fire we could see a light above it, and the shooting went on for a long time. We could hear the shots and the noise and then we started walking towards the area where shots came from. It was dark and then bursts of fire started again, we returned. I -- I hid behind a bush. Nobody could target me from the side and I thought that the others did the same. When I got -- stood up, there was nobody there. And then I got started walking towards the same hilltop. Another burst of fire and then another burst of fire and then I shouted at them, Please don't shoot. I'm one of yours. And I asked him who was there. And he said, Suad. And he said, Wait for me. And then I went up there. There was a guy on the ground and he said, Sir, do you have anything in your back-pack? And I said, I have some bread and some meat. And he said, I have not eaten for three days. And I gave him food and then he had that food, and then he thanked me for having had food and then he said, Let's go. And as we walked, we actually walked on the bodies of dead people. People were crying from the brook and the group went there to collect that person but nobody came back because there was a fire. And then the morning broke above Kamenica. In the meantime I lost Suad. I didn't even know that we were in a Kamenica. And then I recognised Redzo Mehmedovic and I saw that people were being lined up. I was on the right-hand side. I walked behind them and then I met another group from the neighbouring village who asked me, Where are you going -- or, rather, I asked them. And then they said that they were being lined up. I asked if there were any more people there. And they said yes, there are more people, and then we set out towards there. I found a lot of people that I knew from Srebrenica. I asked Amir Gabelic, who was a member of the SUP in Vlasenica before the war, I asked him if he had seen Huso, and he told me that Huso was alive. Everybody told me that Huso was alive but I couldn't find him anywhere. And we were there. There was a paramedic who was dressing the wounds of those who were wounded. Then we were again encircled. They started shooting at us. People scattered. The fire continued and they started calling out to us, Surrender, surrender. Some people started raising their hands with T-shirts in their hands and they encircled us and told us to carry the wounded. And I carried Turkovic Mujo from Masinje [phoen] and his brother was also wounded in the shoulder. We were carrying them. I was not the only one who carried them, and we carried them all the way to the river. We crossed the river and two soldiers were standing there. They searched us. They searched our pockets to see if we had any knives or bombs, and they asked us to open our back-packs to see what is there. They tied our hands behind the back. We crossed an asphalt road and we ended up in the meadow. I didn't know what that was. We were seated in the meadow --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. But let's clarify something, please. In your statement, in your testimony on the 10th of April, 2000, page 2478, you were examined by Mr. Cayley. And there, you said that the Serbs were along the road and they could see you. But that there wasn't any shooting until the point in time when you wanted to cross the road beneath Buljim. Is that correct what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes. There was no shooting for that period. But as to whether they saw us or not, I don't know. I didn't see them. But when we were under Buljim, that's when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you exaggerating with regard to the number of those who were killed and wounded? How many men were wounded and killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: By the stream?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first ambush.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't know whether you would have managed in those conditions to see how many were killed and how many wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the order was issued by your command to carry the wounded with you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: No. But your men surrounded us, they told us to take the wounded with us. That was just above Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But from the beginning, some men were killed. What did you do with the wounded before you were surrounded and what did you do with those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: No one carried away those who were wounded or dead beneath Buljim. It was each man for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you didn't even have any time to bury them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, who would have buried them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened later? Who buried them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that. As to whether they were buried or whether the animals got to them and ate them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were captured you were told to take the wounded and those who had been killed with you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, we were told to take the wounded with us. I did that and another group also Mujo Turkovic away. Nusret was also wounded and he was taken across the river. We put him down by the river. He stayed there. But I saw that Nusret went into a house, and from that point in time onwards, he disappeared without trace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you surrendered or were captured in the area of Lolici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I wasn't captured near Lolici. I was captured above Kamenica, where I was surrounded. We were driven away to Lolici. I didn't know of Kamenica or Lolici. Ramiz Muskic, who survived in Kravica, is the person I asked about where we had been. He said in Lolici. I didn't know that place. If I had known that place, I would have managed to flee somehow. But I didn't know that place at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In part of your testimony you said that there was some confusion. The Muslims also opened fire on each other and until their names were revealed - that was on 16 January 1996, that's what you stated in your statement to the Bosnian authorities - you said that it was only when you heard certain names that you realised there had been some confusion and then the shooting stopped; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, there was the first ambush near Buljim and then another ambush when a Praga weapon was used. So there was some confusion. I don't know who was shooting at the time. I know that this Praga weapon opened fire and that was where there were a lot of men who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that they stopped shooting at you when you said what your name was and then you realised that they were your men?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, how would we have had a Praga weapon in our rear? How would we have used it to open fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. A Praga is not important, but in your statement of the 16th of January, page 3, you said there was some confusion and men were shooting at each other and until the men revealed their names --

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: What sort of names?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any shooting from the group as a result of this confusion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: All I know is that the first ambush had been laid by Buljim. The second ambush in which men were killed -- well, I arrived there at night and I was walking over the bodies there. But as to what happened there, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have some sort of ribbons to identify you? Did you have anything to -- any markings to identify you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: What sort of markings? What sort of identification? Who would have done that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us some of the names of those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I need a break. A short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue. Sir, I take it now you are feeling better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know those people who were killed in your vicinity? Can you give us a few names.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Below Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anywhere.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, how would I know them? All I was thinking about was how to save my life. I wasn't thinking about whether someone was dead or alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there was someone you knew whose name was Senahid. I won't mention his surname.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That was below the place where the second ambush was laid, behind Kamenica, when I was with Suad. He was wearing something that I recognised. He's the only person I recognised. I asked Suad for a light or a match to see him more clearly. I never saw that Suad again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what Senahid's father's name was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Osman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First ambush was by Buljim, the second one by Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, it was above Kamenica somewhere. How am I to know what the name of that area was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Kamenica in the municipality of Bratunac or in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I wouldn't know for sure. I think it's in the municipality of Bratunac. I'm not sure about Zvornik. But I'm more inclined to believe that it is in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one place you saw that there were 20 people who were killed. I'll tell you where that can be found. It was in the early morning on the 13th. I'll tell you where that can be found now. They ran down towards the meadow where the grass was very high -- well, that's Kamenica, in fact. That's the second ambush, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I think that is the first ambush down by the stream. That's where I saw about 20 people who had been killed. They had either been wounded or killed. And at the place where there was the second ambush, there were so many dead people that it was impossible to count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw the number who were killed from the 281st. Did your unit have a lot of losses before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: There were a lot of civilian victims. My daughter was killed from the shrapnel. My cattle was also killed. Two of my neighbours were also killed. And in the neighbouring village, there was one woman who was also killed. There were people who were killed in action. A few people but not many. When Srebrenica fell, they went off in the direction of Potocari and through the woods, and they sustained losses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also know something about weapons, don't you? And if you saw a rifle close-up, you could identify it. If you saw such a weapon from a distance, you wouldn't be able to say exactly what sort of a rifle it was, but you could say that it was an automatic one.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, I'm familiar with the automatic rifles, the M48s and hunting rifles. I was also familiar with these light machine-guns. The 34 light machine-gun. And the 53 light machine-gun. I have heard about the 84 weapon but I never had it in my hands, and I've never seen such a weapon either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw some Serbs, some Serbian soldiers, who had these belts on them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That was in Kravica, in Lolici. There were the regular troops. They were wearing these belts, ammunition belts, and they all wore such belts. From Lolici to Kravica, every 5 metres and on both sides, one could see a soldier. So when we set out in a column from Lolici to Kravica, he said we should advance four abreast in the column. There were -- there was a 53 or an 84 weapon about 50 metres from me, so this person had this machine-gun. And he had a German Shepherd dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The men you saw near the road, they had automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, they had automatic rifles. They were providing security for the road to make sure that no one appeared suddenly. They had these ammunition belts over their chests and automatic rifles and every 6 or 7 metres there was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. You used clips for automatic rifles not ammunition belts. How come they had these ammunition belts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, they had these ammunition belts. We were in a column, four abreast, there was an UNPROFOR transport vehicle, armoured vehicle to the right of us. We passed by it, they didn't react. I don't know who was in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were taken prisoner, you were assembled on a meadow. Is that the meadow that is called Sandici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Sandici or Lolici. Ramzo Muskic said that we were in Lolici. He knew the place. But there were others who were in Sandici. We were taken to Kravica in a column, but there were others who were transported by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you say that there were between 4- and 500 of you there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I didn't count the number of people. I listened to those whispering in front of me. They said there were about 2.000. But I didn't count the -- the number of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning in her summary, Ms. West from Prosecution said that you heard that there were 2.000. Does that mean that that wasn't the conclusion you drew? That's what you heard?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That's what I heard. I heard them whispering that number. There was a teacher and there was a paramedic, and they were whispering and saying that there were 2.000 people. But it never even crossed my mind to count the people there. All I could do was think about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to the information we have, no one was assembled or detained in Lolici. No prisoners. Perhaps they just passed through Lolici, but they were in Sandici. Did General Mladic address you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I know that Ramiz Muskic told me that. I didn't know Kravica, Lolici or Sandici. Where were we, I asked. He said, In Lolici. And General Mladic appeared there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was about half past 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch, but judging by the position of the sun, it was between 1.00 and 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D2253, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the meadow; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: There were more people on the meadow where I was. I don't think there are many people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can't see all of them. That's just some of them. But is that the meadow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't even see some of the houses. There were two houses. One was to the left; the other to the right. And to the left and right, there was a parked tank. And on the tank to the right, there was a PAM, which turned around twice. Someone cried out, Are we going to let him pass through? The other one said, I don't know -- or, rather, he said, Shall we fire? But they didn't fire on us because this other person said, Don't play around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the younger soldier. But the older soldier warned him and told him not to fool around.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: He said, Don't fool around, lower that down. I can't say that he opened fire, but he just turned this barrel around twice. And he said, Shall we let him off?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you were detained there, you recognised some people who could have been from Visnjica or, rather, who were from Visnjica. There was a Serb from Visnjica, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I did not recognise him. There was this fair-haired person and there was someone whom they called Madjarevic. The Madjarevics lived in Visnjica. They said, Search them. So they searched all of them. They took everything, money, gold. I had 11 golden coins. I had 400 francs and 300 German marks. I had ten golden coins. I had two necklaces that belonged to my daughter. And the one with a yellow -- or ponytail took the golden coins, and he asked the other person, What is this? And he said, Put it in your pocket. Don't fool around. They took money from everyone. When they found it, they took gold too. They searched someone they knew. He pleaded with them and asked them to leave them 50 German marks for cigarettes. They said, You'll get your cigarettes. And they took everything they found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P4308. Page 50. We'll show this to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for this document, Witness, before General Mladic appeared, was anyone taken away? Did lorries or buses of any kind arrive to transport these vehicles [as interpreted]? Were you there when General Mladic addressed you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: There were lorries and buses from Potocari. They set off from Potocari with elderly people. Some of the buses passed by as well, and we were there on the meadow, sitting down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your group, was anyone taken away before Mladic appeared or were you all there when Mladic appeared?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: There was only that lorry that went away, that one that was supposed to go to a working organisation, and that's the lorry from which they threw out spades. There was only one person whom I recognised, Fadil Husejnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the screen. You can see the buses and the meadow here. Are you familiar with this area? Could this be the meadow we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Judging by what I see on the screen -- well, there was no forest in the area where we were sitting. As for the asphalt road that links Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, well, that was the first time I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the mid -- the middle of the screen so that the witness can see the detainees and the houses. Can we see the left part of the screen, one-third to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the houses there? And can you see the people across the road? And on the other side, there's a house that was damaged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I can't see a group of people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see these houses to the right, the two or three houses, and then if have a look at the left part, you can see a group of people. It looks like a forest, but these are people.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I can't find my bearings here when looking at the screen. Don't ask me about the forest or the meadow. All I know is that Ramiz Muskic said that the place was called Lolici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this road this far away from you when you saw the buses transporting the civilians?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: The road was near us. It wasn't very far away. And that concerns those who were going from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Madjarevic show you -- was he hospitable, particularly hospitable towards you because he was from Visnjica or did he act in a professional way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: He didn't act provocatively, but the orders they had received was to take money and gold. They searched the people. When they found things they took it away -- they took them away. If they didn't find anything, they couldn't take anything because there was nothing to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We don't need this image on the screen anymore. You said that when you set off you saw Serb civilians and they weren't particularly interested in you and they didn't provoke you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: What do you mean? When we were on the road heading in the direction of Kravica? I only saw those soldiers on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they behaved normally; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: While we were going along the road, no one did anything to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you all walk from that meadow to Kravica or were some transported there by bus?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: All of us who were on the meadow advanced in a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did General Mladic come to the meadow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was. I didn't have a watch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you arrived in Kravica. And you say that at the entrance to the co-operative building, you saw two buses, one closer, one far away, and you had to squeeze between these two buses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: One bus was parked in front of the storehouse, and we had to pass between the warehouse and the bus. There is an asphalt road there. The bus was parked between the warehouse and the asphalt road, and we had to pass between the bus and the warehouse. I went through the first door. Then I went through the second door. I saw that everything was already fully packed. You couldn't find a millimetre of free space. I tried to go through to a corner. There were soldiers standing on both sides of the door, and one of them told me, Sit down. I wanted to lean on the wall because I had pain in my back. When the last man entered the storehouse, he didn't have any room to sit. This one swore at him and he kicked him in the lower back. He said to the soldier, Well, you see, there's no place for me to sit. But he just opened fire, and they were shooting for a long time. There was darkness in the storehouse. People were screaming and crying and asking for help, but who could help us? I just sat close to a man called Salko Redzic of Vlasenica, and we were lying down the whole time. At one point, Salko just shouted, Brother, I am dead. I am killed. And he was hit in the chest with a lot of bullets. Once the shooting stopped, we could hear them outside the storehouse chatting and joking. I had a shirt and a jumper on me, and it was all bloodied, and that's how I arrived in Zepa. I was all covered in blood. And people told me, Keep that jumper. This is going to be a proof. But you know how refugees suffered from the lack of clothing, and eventually this jumper was thrown into the bin because somebody told me that it was not possible to wash it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a little bit confused when you said that it was already fully packed. In your statement given to the state security in Tuzla, you said that the building was yellow and that it was completely empty when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That is not correct. I remember that clearly. I said in my statement that it was fully packed up until the second door. And you may say whatever you wish. I stand by what I saw and experienced. But, sir, you and Mladic are guilty of this. You took over Srebrenica. Why didn't you let people go away? Why did you have to kill them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave it. It's not to us.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to me either.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Can we now have 1D5577.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's your statement given in 1995. October 1995, given in Tuzla when your memory was the most fresh. Now, can we have page 3; the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 in English; and in Serbian, it's the bottom of page 2. So number 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read to you the following. [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] "We arrived in Kravica in the evening and they took us into a building. I heard that was an agricultural warehouse. The building was big with a yellow facade with a porter's lodge on the left of the entrance to the warehouse. The building was completely inside [as interpreted]. We went inside and we had to sit on the concrete floor."

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was. I think it was between 4.00 and 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the transcript, line 15, should read: "The building was completely empty inside."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building to which I came, I said that this building was fully packed as far as the second door. And I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it says here --

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: You can say that there was no one in this building. You can say as well that nobody was killed in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we collapse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where are the people, then, if nobody was killed? They were not killed by lightning in Potocari, or thunder-storm. Anyone can see that, if they wish to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse the English version and zoom in the part ... First, let us -- we do not broadcast this document. Do you see your signature at the bottom of this page, sir? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show him the first page. Do you also see your signature here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the last page. So this must be your statement given to the authority in 1995. Do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with what I had spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to change anything, and I don't want to add anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go back to the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here, you said at the time -- it is written here that the building was completely empty inside. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that very well. Not in a single statement of mine did I say that the building was completely empty. Up until the second door, the area was fully packed with people. But who wrote this, I'm not interested in that. You don't need witnesses to testify to what happened in Potocari. There's a graveyard full of people in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just go back for a moment to the bus that you mentioned. Was there anyone on the bus at that point?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Whether they brought anyone or not, all I saw was the bus. Some people said that people had been driven by buses. I know that I arrived there in a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that bus riddled with bullets whilst you were passing by it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, do you really think that I had time to look and check whether it was damaged by -- by bullets?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't damaged.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Look, man, I don't know. I haven't seen anything. Would you think about anything of that sort if you were in my shoes? I was only concerned about what was -- going to happen to me, whether I would survive or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst you were in the building, were you able to hear or did you hear any shooting around the building, across the small river in the forest?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on outside. I know what was happening inside. However, what was happening in the forest or around the road, I don't know anything about that. All I know is what was happening is -- in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said there were gun-shots outside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes. But there were gun-shots aiming at the doors and the windows. If you look now, would you be able to see what is happening outside at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, before this shooting at windows and doors, did you hear any distant gun-shots around the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Listen, I already told you about this so don't ask me what was happening outside and in the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Don't "very well" me. Don't ask me any questions -- and I can only tell you what was happening inside the storehouse. I didn't see what was going on outside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you saying that there was fire from Zoljas and Osas? Did you see the people firing from those weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of weapons were used. I already said, it was pitch-dark in the warehouse. You couldn't see more than 6 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in this same statement, I think, you said that you had been fired at from Zoljas and Osas.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Well, they fired from all sorts of weapons, although I didn't see them. All I know is that they managed to kill people inside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 3, you say that fire came from Zoljas and Osas. Are you withdrawing and recanting this statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know what they fired from, whether Osas, Zoljas, machine-guns, hand-grenades. All sorts of fire was coming. I just hid in a corner and prayed to God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this shooting cause any fire inside the storehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I didn't see any fires breaking out whilst I was there. I don't know about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted) you said that 2.000 people had been killed but that then, later on, when you spoke with the OTP, you said that was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: That's not what I said. All I said was that I heard that about 2.000 people were in Lolici. And among those who were brought to the warehouse, I survived, and (redacted) also survived but he was later killed in Baljkovica, some 70 days later, he stepped onto a mine. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: (redacted). He jumped through the window and managed to survive and reach Zepa. He spent the whole day lying under the window wounded. And he said that nobody was paying any attention to him because they took him for dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these bodies really covered by hay, as you had heard someone saying that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Whatever bodies were left there were not dragged away. Instead, they were covered with hay, and then they set it on fire. And I was thinking I don't want to be burned alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During that night, was anyone dragging the bodies away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: They did it during day-time, until dusk. When it became dark, they parked the loader and they said, Throw hay across and over the bodies. I think I managed to escape on the night between the 14th and the 15th, together with (redacted). There was a young lad and I pleaded with him to agree to -- for me to join him, but he didn't want to do that. (redacted) and I reached the asphalt road, and then on the right-hand side, somebody said, Stop. But I threw myself onto the ground, and when he shouted at me three times, Get up, get up, and get up, I ran to the river, and I drank some water. (redacted) ran after me but I couldn't communicate with him because he was deaf. And then through a corn field, there was a path there. We reached the river. I again went down to the river to cool myself and to drink some water. The two of us sat under a tree, and then I heard a burst of fire coming from the storehouse, and this one never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just out of an abundance of caution, Ms. West, if you could take a look whether we need a redaction on line 3 -- on previous page. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And may we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need a break, sir? Is it -- are you okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a toothache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more do you have, Mr. Karadzic? Your time is almost up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to finish before the end of the session, but the witness is verbose and he provides lengthy answers and it depends on him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You spent -- you wasted most of your time. And then you say you need more? It is not acceptable. I will consult the Registrar how much time you have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that you have five minutes left, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I'm not in charge of the length of the answers. My questions are very concrete, and the witness could provide short answers. He chooses to provide lengthy answers, and I can't influence that. I can't interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not me who makes things longer than necessary. You are the one who asks me questions that require long answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not argue with you, Mr. Karadzic. You have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct - and, please, provide as short answers as possible - is it true that you stated that some people had survived the shooting on the 13th in the evening and that they were killed on the 14th in the morning? Because on the 14th in the morning, fire was opened again.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: In the morning they asked if there are any survivors and if there were, to come out and to be taken to hospital. A few of them did come out. I don't know how many. I don't know who. I didn't see them. And they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: How do I know? Because fire was opened and from then on nobody ever saw them again. If I had come out, maybe I would have gone missing as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people survived? How many actually responded on the 14th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Sir, I did not count heads. I -- would you have counted head if you were in my shoes at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which asphalt did they wash and why?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know. I suspect there was blood on the asphalt. I'm sure that they didn't wash it because the weather was dry and the asphalt was dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they wash the asphalt on the street or the asphalt in front --

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: In front of the warehouse. There was a tank full of water, and they used the hose to wash the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent 24 hours under the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Perhaps 24 hours, if not longer. And after midnight, when I could no longer hear any voices in front of the warehouse, I started moving. I stood up. And perhaps I spent an hour or so sitting down because I had pins and needles in my legs. And in my arms as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That night, between the 14th and the 15th, you saw the machinery and you say that you could even see the colour because the weather was clear.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the machinery was yellow; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't remember the colour of the machinery. I found myself next to a loader. It was not cloudy. The sky was clear. I did not observe the machinery. I didn't pay much attention to the machinery, but I saw a soldier on the left side. I did not see the soldier on the right side until the moment he actually stopped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in your statement provided on -- in 2003, on the 14th of July, on page 1248, where you say that the vehicles were yellow. And you also said in open session when you were examined by Mr. Cayley on the 10th of April, 2000, on page 2467, that the visibility was good at the time because the sky was clear.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, the sky was, indeed, clear. There was no moonlight. But as for the colours, you can say whatever. That they were green or blue or yellow. I was not interested in any of the colours. All I was interested in was my own life and how to save myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you managed to move from the warehouse. You walked some 200 or 300 metres away. That's what you stated.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: I don't know how far it was but then I heard three bursts of fire near the warehouse and that person from Lolici also never reappeared after that. He went missing forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the sky was clear and then it started raining and you hid --

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
utterances.text: Yes, it started raining during the night. We were still not talking about rain. And when the rain started falling, we hid under a tree. We were wet. The day broke. He was familiar with the terrain. And if he had told me, Let's go to Kravica, I would have followed him because I didn't know where I was. He was dragging me along for five days. I found some persons from Bratunac, Kasim and Sacir, and they told me, Let's go to Zepa. One man from Srebrenica told me that there is -- there's hope in Zepa because Zepa hadn't fallen. The ambushes are not that strong and he said that he knew the road to Baljkovica. He didn't want to Zepa, I didn't want to Baljkovica. I didn't know the road there, and that's how I decided to join Sacir and Kasim, and I went in the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the benefit of the participants, in the statement provided on 14 July 2003, on page 1226, you stated that you moved some 200 to 300 metres from the warehouse, and then you also stated that it started raining. So you were not far from the warehouse and then it started raining from clear skies.

utterances.speaker: KDZ071
